stimulus: Iron remembers. That's the odd thing about a paperclip that gets magnetized by a passing magnet: nothing in its chemistry changed, yet the past is written into it. Physicists draw the hysteresis loop, that fat lopsided curve, and the area inside it is energy lost as the domains snap around, so memory costs heat. Barkhausen noise comes to mind: put a coil around the sample and listen, and you hear crackling as domain walls jump past pinning sites, like a crowd of tiny ratchets. Each crackle is a little decision. Then there are first-order reversal curves, where you saturate, back off to some reversal field, and sweep up again, mapping which grains flipped and which stayed put. It's like interrogating the material with different histories to see which ones it distinguishes. Spin glasses are stranger: the memory-and-rejuvenation experiments where you cool, pause at a temperature, resume, and later on warming the dip in susceptibility reappears, as if the system had kept a hidden ledger of every pause. Return-point memory shows up in Preisach models, a pile of imaginary two-state switches each with its own thresholds. A suspicion lurks: is the stored thing a state, or just slow relaxation, aging that merely looks like remembering? Annealing erases it, shaking with an AC field demagnetizes, and the trouble is that crumpled paper, sheared sand, and charge-density waves all show similar tricks. Even coffee-ground jammed packings seem to remember how they were tapped.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: First-order reversal curve (FORC) stimulation protocols
ideas.description: Drive cells to saturating AP-1 activation (e.g., high-dose TPA or serum/MAPK stimulation), withdraw to varied reversal levels, then re-stimulate, and read out chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene transcription at each step. Mapping which AP-1 sites and genes show path-dependent responses, with return-point memory versus simple relaxation, identifies a history-dependent hysteresis-like state and distinguishes it from the stimulus level alone.

ideas.title: Memory-and-rejuvenation pause experiments with decay-time series
ideas.description: Give a stimulus, pause or wash out for different durations, then restimulate and compare the response with naive cells, tracking FOS/JUN levels, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and enhancer accessibility over time. If the primed response persists long after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, and the persistence is separable from slow relaxation (aging) by varying pause length and temperature, memory is more than a lingering transient.

ideas.title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics, 'Barkhausen' style
ideas.description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN reporters and an AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells across repeated stimulations, resolving discrete bursts and enhancer switching events. Analyze the distribution of switching thresholds across cells, and test whether cells show bistability, with a Preisach-like decomposition into independent two-state loci, each with its own on/off thresholds.

ideas.title: Acute AP-1 degradation as an erasure/demagnetization test
ideas.description: Use degron-tagged or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 at defined times: during priming, during the memory interval, or only at restimulation. Compare this with erasure controls such as a decaying oscillating stimulus (an AC-field analogue), and read out chromatin state and gene expression. If AP-1 is needed only to write the memory, not to maintain it, it is an initiator; if removal during the interval erases the memory, it is a maintainer.

ideas.title: Site-specific mutation and epigenetic readout of pioneer-like AP-1 sites
ideas.description: Edit individual AP-1 motifs in memory-associated enhancers with CRISPR, or block them with dCas9, and measure whether priming-induced accessibility, H3K27ac, and enhanced re-induction are lost, using ATAC-seq, ChIP/CUT&Tag for histone marks and SWI/SNF (BAF), and nascent RNA. Combine with a chromatin-state perturbation, such as a BAF inhibitor, to test whether the stored thing is a self-sustaining chromatin state or only slow relaxation of AP-1 itself.
